questions.question: How would you type a React component's props when some props are mutually exclusive (e.g., either href or onClick, but not both)?
questions.answer: Plain object typing (`{ href？: string; onClick?: () => void }`) allows both, neither, or either — TypeScript won't catch a caller passing both. To make combinations mutually exclusive, model props as a discriminated union: define two separate shapes and union them, e.g. `type LinkProps = { as: 'link'; href: string; onClick?: never } | { as: 'button'; onClick: () => void; href?: never }`, so a discriminant field (or the mere presence/absence of a required field) lets TypeScript narrow which variant applies and reject invalid combinations at the call site. A lighter-weight version without an explicit discriminant uses `Exclude`-style 'never' props on the sibling variant (`{ href: string; onClick?: never } | { href?: never; onClick: () => void }`) so providing both produces a type error. The general principle senior candidates are expected to articulate: use the type system to make invalid states unrepresentable, rather than relying on runtime checks or comments.

questions.question: How do you correctly type a custom hook's return value, especially when returning a tuple like useState does?
questions.answer: If a hook returns an array intended to be destructured positionally (mirroring `useState`'s `[value, setValue]` convention), TypeScript by default infers the return type as a general array (`(T | U)[]`), which loses positional typing when destructured. The fix is to explicitly annotate the return type as a tuple, either via an `as const` assertion on the returned array literal or an explicit function return type annotation like `function useToggle(): [boolean, () => void] { ... }`. If the hook returns several loosely related values, an object return (`{ value, setValue, reset }`) is usually clearer and self-documenting than a tuple, since object properties are accessed by name rather than position, and TypeScript infers object return types correctly without extra annotation. The general rule: use a tuple only when order is meaningful and there are few values (as with `useState`); prefer a named object otherwise.

questions.question: How would you type a generic reusable component (e.g., a <Select<T>> that works with any option type)?
questions.answer: Declare the component as a generic function component: `function Select<T>(props: { options: T[]; value: T; onChange: (value: T) => void; getLabel: (option: T) => string }) { ... }`. TypeScript infers `T` from how the component is used (`<Select options={users} value={selectedUser} onChange={setUser} getLabel={u => u.name} />` infers `T = User`), giving full type safety on `value`, `onChange`, and any render-prop callbacks without the consumer writing explicit type arguments in most cases. One caveat: arrow-function components don't support generics as cleanly in `.tsx` files because `<T>` is ambiguous with JSX syntax — you either need `<T,>(props) => ...` (a trailing comma) or, more commonly, just use a regular `function` declaration, which avoids the ambiguity entirely and is generally preferred for generic components.

questions.question: What TypeScript utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record) come up most often when typing component props, and what's a case where you'd reach for each?
questions.answer: `Partial<T>` makes all properties of `T` optional — useful for an 'update' function or a component accepting default/override props where only some fields need to be provided (e.g., a form's initial values). `Pick<T, K>` selects a subset of properties from a larger type — useful when a component only needs a few fields from a large domain model (`Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>` for a compact user badge component) so the component's prop type doesn't force the caller to have the entire object. `Omit<T, K>` is the inverse — take an existing type and remove specific keys — commonly used when a component wraps a native element and forwards most of its props except one or two it overrides itself (`Omit<React.ComponentProps<'button'>, 'onClick'> & { onClick: (id: string) => void }`). `Record<K, V>` builds an object type with a specific key set mapped to a value type — useful for lookup/config objects, like a `Record<'small' | 'medium' | 'large', string>` mapping a `size` prop to CSS classes.

questions.question: Why is PropTypes considered legacy in a TypeScript codebase, and what changed with React 19 dropping it from the core package?
questions.answer: PropTypes was React's runtime prop-type checker: you declared expected shapes, and React logged a console warning in development if a mismatch occurred at render time. In a TypeScript codebase this is largely redundant — TypeScript catches the same category of mismatches at compile time, before the code even runs, with editor integration (autocomplete, inline errors, refactor-safety) that a runtime-only check can't provide, and with zero runtime cost in production. As of React 19, `PropTypes` support has been removed from the `react` package entirely (using `Component.propTypes` is a silent no-op), officially reflecting that TypeScript (or Flow) is the recommended path for prop validation going forward. Teams still using JavaScript without a type checker either accept the reduced safety or need to migrate to TypeScript to get equivalent guarantees.

questions.question: How do you correctly type a DOM event handler in React (e.g., an onChange on an <input>) with TypeScript?
questions.answer: React re-exports typed wrappers around native DOM events as generic types parameterized by the target element, since the `event.target` type depends on which element the handler is attached to. For an input's change event: `function handleChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) { console.log(e.target.value); }` — the generic parameter (`HTMLInputElement`) ensures `e.target` is correctly typed with `.value`, `.checked`, etc., rather than the generic `EventTarget`. Similar patterns apply to other common handlers: `React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>` for a button click, `React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>` for form submission, `React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>` for key events. These are 'synthetic events' — React's cross-browser wrapper around native events — and are distinct from (though closely mirror) the native DOM event types like `Event`/`MouseEvent` from the DOM lib; mixing them up (e.g., typing a React handler's parameter as the native `MouseEvent`) is a common mistake that produces subtly wrong property access.

questions.question: What is the Actions API introduced in React 19, and what problem does it solve for form submissions and mutations?
questions.answer: Before React 19, handling an async form submission or mutation typically required manually wiring up separate `useState` calls for pending/loading state, the result or error, and disabling the submit button while in flight — boilerplate repeated across every form. React 19's Actions let you pass an async function directly to a `<form>`'s `action` prop (or trigger it inside a transition via `useTransition`), and React automatically manages the pending state, coordinates it with concurrent rendering (so the UI doesn't show intermediate/inconsistent states), handles the result, and — combined with `<Suspense>` and error boundaries — surfaces errors and loading states without hand-written state juggling. Actions are the general primitive; `useActionState`, `useFormStatus`, and `useOptimistic` are hooks built on top of it for specific common needs (state tied to the action's result, reading a parent form's pending status from a child, and optimistic UI, respectively). A Server Action is specifically an Action defined with the `'use server'` directive, allowing it to run on the server when invoked from client code.

questions.question: What does useActionState do, and how does it differ from just tracking loading/error state manually with useState?
questions.answer: `useActionState(actionFn, initialState)` wraps an action and returns `[state, formAction, isPending]`: `state` is the latest value returned by the action (e.g., a validation-error object or success message), `formAction` is the wrapped function you actually pass to the form's `action` prop (or a button's `formAction`), and `isPending` reflects whether the action is currently in flight. Compared to manually tracking this with `useState` (separate `error`, `loading`, and `result` state variables, plus a wrapper function to set them before/after the async call), `useActionState` couples the pending flag directly to the action's execution lifecycle managed by React's own scheduler, works correctly with concurrent rendering and Suspense, and — critically — works during server rendering/progressive enhancement, since the action can run as a real form submission before JavaScript has hydrated. It reduces a repetitive pattern (three or four `useState` calls plus manual try/catch wiring) to a single hook call with a state-updating action function.

questions.question: What is useOptimistic for, and what happens to the optimistic value if the underlying action fails?
questions.answer: `useOptimistic(state, updateFn)` lets you render an 'expected' version of some state immediately while an async action (like a server mutation) is still in flight, rather than waiting for the round-trip before updating the UI — e.g., showing a new comment appear instantly when the user submits it, before the server has confirmed it was saved. You call the returned `addOptimistic` function with the optimistic value, which the `updateFn` merges into a temporary render of `state`; once the underlying action settles (the real state update completes), React automatically reverts the optimistic value to whatever the real, confirmed state is. If the action fails, the optimistic value is discarded and the UI reverts to the last confirmed state — the hook itself doesn't retry or show an error, so the calling code is still responsible for surfacing failure feedback (e.g., a toast, or re-showing the item as 'failed to send') based on the action's own error handling.

questions.question: How does useFormStatus let a deeply nested child (like a submit button) know its parent form is submitting, without prop drilling?
questions.answer: `useFormStatus()` (from `react-dom`) reads the pending/submitting status of the nearest ancestor `<form>` that uses an Action, without the parent needing to pass a `isSubmitting` prop down through every intermediate component. It returns an object including `pending` (boolean), and in some cases `data`, `method`, and `action` reflecting the in-flight submission. A typical use is a reusable `<SubmitButton>` component used across many different forms — it calls `useFormStatus()` internally and disables itself / shows a spinner whenever `pending` is true, with zero coupling to whatever specific form renders it. One important caveat: `useFormStatus` must be called from a component that is a child of the `<form>`, not the component that renders the `<form>` itself — calling it in the same component as the form tag won't see that form's own status.

questions.question: What does the use() hook do, and how is it different from useContext or useEffect for reading a promise?
questions.answer: `use()` reads the value of a resource — currently a Promise or a Context — and, unlike other hooks, can be called conditionally and inside loops, because it isn't a traditional hook constrained by call-order rules; it's designed to integrate with control flow. Passed a Context, `use(SomeContext)` behaves like `useContext` but can be called inside an `if` block. Passed a Promise, `use()` will suspend the component (triggering the nearest `<Suspense>` fallback) until the promise resolves, then return its resolved value directly in that render — no manual `useState`/`useEffect` combo needed to track loading and store the result. This is different from `useEffect` + `fetch`, which requires you to write your own pending/error/data state machine and doesn't naturally integrate with Suspense; `use()` shifts data-loading state management to the Suspense boundary itself. A key constraint: you should not create a new promise directly in a component's render body and pass it to `use()`, since that recreates the promise (and refetches) on every render — the promise should come from a cache, a Server Component, or a stable source outside the render.

questions.question: What is the React Compiler, and what manual optimization patterns does it aim to make unnecessary?
questions.answer: The React Compiler is a build-time tool (reaching stable v1.0 in October 2025) that automatically analyzes component code and inserts memoization — equivalent to what you'd hand-write with `useMemo`, `useCallback`, and `React.memo` — based on React's rules (assuming components and hooks follow the Rules of React, e.g., no mutating props/state directly). Its goal is to make manual memoization largely unnecessary for the common case: instead of developers deciding case-by-case which values/functions/components need wrapping to avoid unnecessary re-renders, the compiler determines this automatically at build time by understanding data dependencies. This doesn't eliminate the underlying concepts (referential stability, avoiding unnecessary re-renders is still what's happening under the hood) — it just removes the manual bookkeeping. Teams adopting it still benefit from understanding why re-renders happen, since profiling and debugging still requires that mental model, and the compiler can silently produce no benefit (or bail out) if code doesn't follow React's rules (e.g., relies on hooks called conditionally, or mutates state/props).

questions.question: What's the difference between a Server Component and a Client Component, and what can/can't each one do?
questions.answer: Server Components (the default in RSC-enabled frameworks like Next.js's App Router) execute exclusively on the server, at request or build time — their code, and any server-only dependencies they import, never get shipped to the browser, which shrinks the client bundle. They can directly access server-only resources (databases, the filesystem, secret API keys, server-only npm packages) without needing a separate API layer, but they cannot use browser-only APIs, React state (`useState`), effects (`useEffect`), or event handlers (`onClick`) — there's no client-side re-render cycle for them to hook into. Client Components, opted into with a `'use client'` directive at the top of the file, are the ones that get bundled and hydrated in the browser, and are where interactivity, state, effects, and browser APIs (`localStorage`, `window`) live. A typical app composes both: Server Components fetch data and render static/structural content, passing serializable props down to Client Components that need interactivity — but a Server Component can never be imported into the middle of a Client Component's subtree (though it can be passed as `children`).

questions.question: What is a Server Action (a function marked 'use server'), and how does it get invoked from a client form?
questions.answer: A Server Action is a function marked with the `'use server'` directive (at the top of the function or the file) that is guaranteed to execute on the server, even when called from client-side code. When you pass a Server Action as a `<form>`'s `action` prop, React automatically wires it up to work as a real HTML form submission — the browser can POST to it even before JavaScript has hydrated (progressive enhancement) — and when a Server Action is invoked from within a form context, React automatically provides the submitted `FormData` object as its first argument. Under the hood, the framework (e.g., Next.js) generates a reference the client can call, which triggers a request to the server, executes the actual function there (with access to databases, secrets, etc.), and returns the result (or an updated state, when paired with `useActionState`) back to the client to update the UI — without the developer manually building a REST/GraphQL endpoint for that mutation.

questions.question: How does React Router's useNavigate differ from just changing window.location, and why does it matter for SPA behavior?
questions.answer: Setting `window.location.href` (or calling `window.location.assign`) triggers a full browser navigation: the page unloads, the browser requests a new document from the server, and the entire JS app re-initializes from scratch — losing all in-memory React state and re-downloading/re-executing the bundle. `useNavigate()` returns a function that performs client-side ('soft') navigation instead: React Router updates the URL via the History API, matches the new route, and re-renders only the parts of the component tree that changed — no full page reload, no state loss outside what the route change itself is meant to reset. This is the entire point of a single-page app: instant transitions without a network round-trip for the shell. `navigate(path)` pushes a new history entry by default; `navigate(path, { replace: true })` replaces the current entry instead (useful after a redirect, like post-login, so the back button doesn't return to the intermediate page); `navigate(-1)` goes back, mirroring `history.back()`.

questions.question: How would you implement a protected/private route that redirects unauthenticated users in React Router?
questions.answer: The common pattern is a wrapper component that checks auth status and either renders its children (or an `<Outlet />` for nested protected routes) or redirects: `function ProtectedRoute({ children }) { const { user } = useAuth(); if (!user) return <Navigate to="/login" replace />; return children; }`, then wrap protected routes with it: `<Route element={<ProtectedRoute><Dashboard /></ProtectedRoute>} />`, or for a whole nested group, `<Route element={<ProtectedRoute><Outlet /></ProtectedRoute>}><Route path="dashboard" .../></Route>`. Using `<Navigate replace>` (rather than `push`) avoids leaving the protected URL in browser history so the back button doesn't loop the user back to a page they can't access. For a better UX, the redirect target should typically remember the originally-requested path (e.g., via `state={{ from: location }}` passed to `<Navigate>`) so after a successful login the user is sent back to where they intended to go, rather than always to a default landing page. It's also worth noting this is purely a UI/UX concern — the actual authorization must still be enforced server-side, since client-side route guards can be bypassed by anyone with dev tools.

questions.question: How do nested routes and layout routes work in React Router (or Next.js's App Router), and why are they useful for shared UI like navbars?
questions.answer: In React Router v6+, routes can be nested by declaring child `<Route>` elements inside a parent, and the parent's `element` renders an `<Outlet />` wherever it wants the matched child route's content to appear: `<Route path="dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}><Route path="analytics" element={<Analytics />} /><Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} /></Route>` — `DashboardLayout` renders a shared sidebar/navbar once, with `<Outlet />` swapping in `Analytics` or `Settings` as the URL changes, without those child components needing to re-implement the shared chrome. An `index` route (no `path`, just `index`) defines what renders at the parent's own path when no child segment matches. Next.js's App Router applies the same idea via the filesystem: a `layout.tsx` file wraps all routes in its directory and persists across navigations within that segment, while `page.tsx` files are swapped. The benefit either way is avoiding duplicated layout code across every page and, since the layout component itself doesn't remount on child navigation, preserving its own state (like scroll position or open menus) across route changes within that section.

questions.question: How would you read and update query/search parameters in the URL using React Router?
questions.answer: `useSearchParams()` (mirroring `useState`'s API shape) returns `[searchParams, setSearchParams]`: `searchParams` is a `URLSearchParams` instance you read via `.get('key')`, `.getAll('key')`, or iterate over, and `setSearchParams({ key: 'value' })` (or passing a `URLSearchParams` instance, or an updater function) replaces the query string and triggers a re-render with the new values — this is a client-side navigation under the hood, so it updates the URL bar and browser history without a full reload. A common pattern is syncing a filter/search UI to the URL so state survives a refresh or is shareable via link: read the current filter from `searchParams.get('sort') ?? 'default'` on render, and call `setSearchParams` when the user changes the filter. Note that `useSearchParams` only manages the query string of the current route — to navigate to a different path while also setting query params, you typically build the target with `useNavigate` (e.g., `navigate({ pathname: '/results', search: '?q=' + query })`) instead.

questions.question: When would you choose Redux Toolkit over Zustand (or vice versa) for a new project's state management?
questions.answer: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the right fit when a project needs strict, predictable, testable state transitions at scale — it enforces the reducer/action pattern, integrates tightly with Redux DevTools for time-travel debugging, pairs naturally with RTK Query for server-state caching, and has broad team familiarity in many orgs, which matters for onboarding and consistency on larger teams or codebases with complex, cross-cutting state logic. Zustand is a much smaller, less opinionated store: no boilerplate actions/reducers required (you just write functions that call `set`), no context provider needed, hooks-based selectors that avoid Context's broad re-render problem by default, and a much smaller bundle/API surface — it tends to be preferred for small-to-mid apps, libraries, or teams that want minimal ceremony and don't need Redux's strict unidirectional conventions or its ecosystem (middleware, DevTools time-travel). In practice the decision often comes down to team preference and existing investment rather than a hard technical requirement, since both handle typical client-state needs well; RTK's stronger structure pays off more as state logic complexity and team size grow.

questions.question: What problem do libraries like TanStack Query or SWR solve that a general-purpose state store (Redux/Zustand) doesn't handle well?
questions.answer: General-purpose client-state stores are built for state your app owns and mutates directly; server data is fundamentally different — it's a cached, potentially stale copy of something owned elsewhere, that can change without your app's knowledge and needs to be kept in sync over time. TanStack Query/SWR are purpose-built for that: they handle request deduplication (multiple components requesting the same data fire one network call), automatic background refetching (on window focus, network reconnect, or interval), caching with configurable staleness (`staleTime`) and garbage collection (`gcTime`) so repeated navigations reuse cached data instead of re-fetching, built-in loading/error states per query, retry logic with backoff, and pagination/infinite-scroll helpers — all without hand-writing that logic into a Redux slice or Zustand store. Rolling this yourself in a general store is possible but means reimplementing cache invalidation, staleness, and race-condition handling from scratch; these libraries exist specifically because 'server state' has different lifecycle requirements than 'client state.'

questions.question: What is normalized state shape in Redux, and why is it preferred over deeply nested state for relational data?
questions.answer: Normalized state stores relational/entity data the way a relational database would: each entity type gets a flat lookup table keyed by ID (`{ users: { byId: { '1': {...} }, allIds: ['1', '2'] } }`) rather than nested inside each other (`{ posts: [{ id: 1, author: { id: 5, name: '...', posts: [...] } }] }`). The nested form duplicates data (the same user object embedded in multiple posts) and makes updates error-prone — updating a user's name in one nested copy doesn't update the others unless you carefully find and update every occurrence. The normalized form stores each entity exactly once; updating it in one place is reflected everywhere it's referenced (since other entities just hold the ID, not a copy). It also makes lookups O(1) by ID instead of requiring array scans, and simplifies reducer logic since each slice only needs to handle its own entity type. Redux Toolkit's `createEntityAdapter` is the standard tool for generating normalized CRUD reducers and selectors without hand-writing this boilerplate.

questions.question: How does RTK Query (or TanStack Query) handle cache invalidation after a mutation, and why does that matter for keeping UI in sync?
questions.answer: In TanStack Query, after a mutation succeeds you explicitly call `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })` (typically inside the mutation's `onSuccess` callback) — this marks any cached queries matching that key as stale and triggers an automatic background refetch for any currently-mounted component observing that data, so the UI reflects the server's new state without a manual page refresh or prop-drilled 'refresh' callback. Invalidation is distinct from a blind refetch: it's 'smart' in that it only refetches queries that actually have active observers (mounted components using them) right now, deferring others until they're next observed. RTK Query uses a related but declaratively-configured mechanism — endpoints declare `providesTags` (which cache entries they represent) and `invalidatesTags` (which tags a mutation should invalidate), and RTK Query automatically triggers refetches for any query providing a tag that a completed mutation invalidates, without manually listing query keys at each call site. Both approaches solve the same core problem: without some invalidation mechanism, a successful mutation leaves stale cached reads showing old data until the cache's normal staleness/TTL expires on its own.

questions.question: What's the difference between controlled form libraries like Formik and 'uncontrolled-by-default' ones like React Hook Form, and why does that distinction affect performance on large forms?
questions.answer: Formik is built around controlled inputs: every field's value lives in React state, so each keystroke updates state and re-renders the form (or, depending on structure, the whole form tree) to keep the input's displayed value in sync. React Hook Form instead defaults to uncontrolled inputs — it registers refs to the DOM nodes via a `register()` function and reads their values directly from the DOM (typically on blur, change, or submit) rather than storing every keystroke in React state, which means most keystrokes don't trigger a React re-render of the form at all. On a small form the difference is imperceptible, but on a large form with dozens of fields, complex conditional rendering, or expensive validation, Formik's controlled-everywhere approach can cause noticeably more re-render work per keystroke, while React Hook Form's approach keeps typing responsive since state/re-renders are only involved when actually needed (e.g., showing a validation error). This is the primary reason React Hook Form is often recommended for performance-sensitive or very large forms, though both are capable, well-maintained libraries with similar validation and TypeScript integration (often paired with schema validators like Zod or Yup).

questions.question: How would you implement client-side form validation that shows field-level errors on blur but not on every keystroke?
questions.answer: Track two pieces of state per field (or per form, depending on library): the current value, and whether the field has been 'touched' (has the user left it at least once) — validation errors are only displayed when `touched && hasError`, so errors don't flash while the user is still mid-typing on their first pass through the field. Concretely: an `onBlur` handler sets `touched: true` for that field (and can trigger validation at that point), while `onChange` just updates the value (and, once a field is already touched, can re-validate live so the error clears as soon as the user fixes it — a common UX refinement: validate strictly on blur first, but validate on every change after the first error has been shown, so corrections are acknowledged immediately). Both React Hook Form (`mode: 'onBlur'`, or `reValidateMode: 'onChange'`) and Formik (tracking `touched`/`errors` from `useFormik`) support this pattern natively via configuration rather than requiring you to hand-roll the touched-state bookkeeping.

questions.question: How would you handle a multi-step form (a wizard) while preserving state across steps and supporting back/forward navigation?
questions.answer: Keep all the form data in state that lives above the individual step components (a parent wizard component's `useState`/`useReducer`, or a form-library instance created once at the wizard level) rather than inside each step, so navigating between steps doesn't lose data entered on a previous step. Track the current step index separately from the data, and render only the active step's fields, passing the shared state (and an update function) down as props — each step component reads its relevant slice and writes back to the shared object rather than owning independent local state. For back/forward navigation, decide whether step transitions should also change the URL (e.g., `/checkout/shipping`, `/checkout/payment` via React Router) — doing so lets the browser's back/forward buttons and refresh work naturally and makes each step linkable/bookmarkable, at the cost of needing to guard against a user directly navigating to a later step's URL before completing earlier ones (a step-completion/validation gate). If the wizard shouldn't be a real navigable route, an internal step index with your own 'Back'/'Next' buttons (and disabling 'Next' until the current step validates) is simpler. Persisting in-progress data to `sessionStorage`/`localStorage` protects against accidental refreshes losing everything.

questions.question: How do you manage keyboard focus when opening and closing a modal so it stays accessible to screen reader and keyboard-only users?
questions.answer: When a modal opens, focus should move into it — typically to the first focusable element or a designated element like the close button or heading — using a ref and calling `.focus()` in a `useEffect` that runs when the modal's open state becomes true. While open, focus needs to be trapped inside the modal: Tab and Shift+Tab should cycle only among the modal's own focusable elements rather than escaping to content behind it (which is often also hidden from assistive tech via `aria-hidden`/`inert` on the rest of the page). When the modal closes, focus should be restored to the element that originally triggered it (typically the button that opened the modal) — save a ref to that element before opening, and call `.focus()` on it in the modal's cleanup/close handler — otherwise keyboard/screen-reader users lose their place in the page entirely. The modal itself should use `role="dialog"` (or `alertdialog`) with `aria-modal="true"` and an accessible name (`aria-labelledby` pointing at its heading), and Escape should close it. Rather than hand-rolling focus trapping, most production code relies on a tested library or primitive (Radix UI's Dialog, React Aria, `focus-trap-react`) since the edge cases (focusable-but-hidden elements, dynamically added content) are easy to get subtly wrong.

questions.question: What's the difference between aria-live="polite" and aria-live="assertive", and when would you use each for dynamic content announcements?
questions.answer: `aria-live` marks a region of the page whose content changes should be announced by screen readers even when it isn't the user's current focus. `polite` (the more common choice) tells the screen reader to finish whatever it's currently saying and wait for a natural pause before announcing the update — appropriate for non-critical, non-urgent updates like a 'saved' confirmation, a chat message arriving, a search result count changing, or form validation summaries. `assertive` interrupts whatever the screen reader is currently announcing to speak the update immediately — reserved for urgent, time-sensitive information the user must know right away, like a session-expiry warning, a critical error blocking further action, or a countdown about to time out an action. Overusing `assertive` is a common accessibility mistake since it disrupts the user's flow and can make an app feel chaotic to navigate with a screen reader; `polite` should be the default unless there's a genuine reason interruption is warranted.

questions.question: Why can't you rely solely on div/span with click handlers for interactive elements, and what accessibility problems does that cause?
questions.answer: A `<div onClick={...}>` looks clickable visually but is invisible to assistive technology as an interactive control by default: it has no implicit ARIA role (so screen readers announce it as plain text/group, not a 'button'), it isn't in the keyboard tab order (no default `tabIndex`), it doesn't respond to Enter/Space the way a native `<button>` does, and it has no built-in focus indicator or disabled-state handling. This excludes keyboard-only users (who can't reach or activate it at all) and screen-reader users (who won't know it's actionable). If you must build a custom interactive element rather than using semantic HTML, you have to manually replicate everything the browser gives native elements for free: an appropriate `role` (`button`, `link`, etc.), `tabIndex={0}` to make it focusable, `onKeyDown` handlers for Enter/Space (or the specific key(s) that role expects), visible focus styling, and `aria-disabled`/`aria-pressed` etc. as relevant. The strongly preferred fix is simply to use the real semantic element (`<button>`, `<a href>`) whenever the styling constraint that pushed someone toward a `div` can be solved with CSS instead.

questions.question: How would you make a custom dropdown or combobox component accessible, including arrow-key navigation and aria-expanded?
questions.answer: Follow the ARIA combobox/listbox pattern: the trigger/input gets `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded` toggled to reflect whether the option list is open, `aria-controls` pointing at the listbox's `id`, and (for a searchable combobox) `aria-autocomplete`. The option list itself gets `role="listbox"`, with each option as `role="option"` and `aria-selected` marking the current/highlighted one. Keyboard behavior: ArrowDown/ArrowUp move a 'highlighted' option (tracked in state, not actual DOM focus — focus typically stays on the input while `aria-activedescendant` on the input points at the highlighted option's `id`, so screen readers announce the right option without moving real focus away from the text field); Enter selects the highlighted option and closes the list; Escape closes the list without selecting; Home/End jump to first/last option. The trigger should also close the list on blur/click-outside, and closing it shouldn't require a mouse. This is enough surface area that many teams reach for a tested headless implementation (Radix, React Aria, Headless UI, Downshift) rather than hand-rolling every ARIA relationship and key handler correctly from scratch.

questions.question: What accessibility issues are specific to single-page app routing (e.g., focus not moving to new content, route changes not being announced), and how would you address them?
questions.answer: Traditional multi-page sites give assistive tech two things 'for free' on every navigation: the browser resets focus to the top of the document, and screen readers announce the new page's title. Client-side routing bypasses both — the DOM just updates in place, so a screen reader user who navigated via a link may have no indication the page 'changed' at all, and sighted keyboard users' focus stays wherever it was (often now pointing at a stale or removed element). The standard fix is to manage this manually on route change: move focus to a sensible landmark — commonly the page's `<h1>` (given `tabIndex={-1}` so it's programmatically focusable without being in the normal tab order) — inside a `useEffect` keyed on the route/location changing, and update `document.title` per route so both sighted users (browser tab) and screen readers (which often announce title changes) get a signal that navigation occurred. Some teams also add a visually-hidden `aria-live="polite"` region that announces 'Navigated to [Page Name]' on route change for extra clarity. Frameworks like Next.js and libraries like `@reach/router`/Gatsby have historically shipped some of this focus-management behavior built in, but it's not universal or automatic in a plain React Router setup, so it needs verifying.

questions.question: What precautions would you take before using dangerouslySetInnerHTML with content that isn't fully trusted?
questions.answer: First, avoid it if there's any alternative — often 'rich content' can be modeled as structured data and rendered with real JSX/components instead of raw HTML strings, which sidesteps the risk entirely. If raw HTML genuinely must be rendered (e.g., a markdown-to-HTML pipeline, or user-generated rich text), run the string through a dedicated, actively-maintained sanitization library (DOMPurify is the standard choice) that strips dangerous elements/attributes (`<script>`, inline event handlers like `onerror`, `javascript:` URLs) while preserving safe formatting tags — writing a custom regex-based sanitizer yourself is a well-known way to miss edge cases attackers know how to exploit. Sanitize as close to render time as practical (or at minimum, treat sanitization as mandatory server-side too, not just client-side, since a client-only check can be bypassed by calling the API directly), pair it with a Content-Security-Policy that restricts script sources as defense-in-depth, and keep the sanitization library itself updated, since XSS bypass techniques for HTML sanitizers are an ongoing cat-and-mouse game.

questions.question: How would you implement a protected route or role-based UI so that unauthorized users can't even see restricted components, not just get blocked by the backend?
questions.answer: At the routing layer, use a guard component (as with the earlier protected-route pattern) that checks not just 'is the user authenticated' but also 'does the user's role/permissions satisfy this route's requirement,' redirecting to a login or an 'access denied' page otherwise — e.g., `<RequireRole role="admin"><AdminPanel /></RequireRole>`. Within a page, role-based UI elements (an 'Edit' button, an admin-only settings section) should be conditionally rendered based on the current user's permissions held in auth state/context, rather than always rendering and trying to disable/hide via CSS (which a user could still inspect or reveal via dev tools) — genuinely not mounting the component means its code, data, and any props it might have received aren't present in the DOM or React tree at all. It's important to be explicit that this is a UX/usability layer, not a security boundary: hiding a component client-side prevents accidental exposure and confusing UI, but a determined user can still call the underlying API directly, so every privileged action and every piece of sensitive data must also be authorized server-side, independent of what the client chooses to render.

questions.question: Where should you store an auth token (memory, localStorage, httpOnly cookie) in a React SPA, and what are the security trade-offs of each?
questions.answer: localStorage/sessionStorage: simple to use and persists across reloads (localStorage) or tabs' lifetime (sessionStorage), but is fully accessible to any JavaScript running on the page — meaning a successful XSS attack (e.g., via an unsanitized `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or a compromised third-party script) can read and exfiltrate the token directly. In-memory (e.g., a variable in a store, not persisted): not accessible via storage APIs and cleared automatically on tab close/reload (which is a UX cost — the user has to re-authenticate on every reload unless paired with a silent refresh flow), and still readable by injected JS if XSS occurs while the token is in memory, though the attack surface/window is smaller than persistent storage. httpOnly cookies: set by the server with the `HttpOnly` flag, meaning JavaScript cannot read them at all (immune to token theft via XSS), and the browser automatically attaches them to requests to the matching domain — but this shifts the risk to CSRF (since the browser sends the cookie automatically on any request, including ones triggered by a malicious site), which must be mitigated separately (`SameSite=Strict/Lax` cookies, CSRF tokens, or checking custom request headers the browser won't auto-attach cross-origin). Most current guidance favors httpOnly, SameSite cookies (often paired with a short-lived access token plus a longer-lived refresh mechanism) as the strongest default, precisely because it removes the token from JS-reachable storage entirely.

questions.question: What causes an unbounded bundle size in a growing React app, and what tools/techniques would you use to diagnose and reduce it?
questions.answer: Common causes: importing entire libraries when only a small piece is used (e.g., importing all of Lodash instead of a single function), accidentally bundling server-only or dev-only code into the client bundle, duplicate versions of the same dependency pulled in by different packages, large third-party libraries (heavy chart/date libraries, moment.js instead of a lighter alternative) chosen without checking their size cost, and simply not code-splitting — shipping every route/feature in a single bundle instead of loading it on demand. To diagnose: use a bundle analyzer (`source-map-explorer`, `webpack-bundle-analyzer`, or Vite's `rollup-plugin-visualizer`) to see a treemap of what's actually contributing to bundle size, and check whether tree-shaking is actually working (some libraries aren't ESM-friendly and pull in more than expected). Fixes include route-level and component-level code splitting with `React.lazy`/dynamic `import()`, swapping heavy dependencies for lighter alternatives, ensuring imports are granular (`import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'` rather than `import _ from 'lodash'`, or using a tree-shakeable package), and auditing for duplicate dependency versions via the bundler's dependency graph output.

questions.question: How does list virtualization (e.g., react-window) improve performance for rendering thousands of rows, and what does it give up compared to rendering everything?
questions.answer: Virtualization (windowing) renders only the rows currently visible in the viewport (plus a small overscan buffer above/below), rather than mounting DOM nodes for every item in a list that might have thousands of entries — the container tracks scroll position and swaps which data maps to the small set of actually-rendered rows as the user scrolls, using absolute positioning to simulate the full scrollable height. This dramatically reduces the number of DOM nodes React has to create, diff, and keep in memory, which is the main performance bottleneck for very long lists (both initial render time and scroll responsiveness). The trade-off: the browser's native in-page find (Ctrl+F) won't find text in rows that aren't currently rendered; SEO/crawlers relying on full static HTML won't see off-screen content; scroll-to-item and dynamic row heights need extra handling (measuring and caching heights, since the library can't know an item's size until it's rendered at least once); and it adds implementation complexity compared to a plain `.map()`. `react-window` is the modern, smaller successor to the older `react-virtualized`, and is generally preferred unless a project needs a legacy feature only `react-virtualized` still supports.

questions.question: How would you implement virtualizing a list where each row has a different, dynamically-measured height?
questions.answer: Fixed-size virtualization (`FixedSizeList` in react-window) is simple because the library can compute any row's offset directly from a constant row height. Variable-height virtualization is harder because the library can't know an item's real height until it has actually been rendered and measured at least once — so implementations typically use a component like react-window's `VariableSizeList`, seeded with an estimated height per row, and update a cache of real measured heights (via `ResizeObserver` or a ref callback that reads `getBoundingClientRect()` after render) once each row is actually rendered, calling the list's `resetAfterIndex` method to tell it to recompute offsets below the changed row. This means the scrollbar/scroll position can shift slightly as more accurate measurements come in during scrolling (a known UX rough edge of dynamic-height virtualization). Libraries like `react-virtualized-auto-sizer` (for making the list fill its container responsively) and dedicated caching utilities are commonly combined with this to manage the added complexity, and some newer libraries (e.g., `@tanstack/react-virtual`) are built from the ground up with dynamic measurement as a first-class case rather than an add-on.

questions.question: What's the difference between debouncing and throttling, and which would you use for a scroll handler versus a search input?
questions.answer: Debouncing delays execution until a burst of events— each new event resets the timer, so the function only runs once, after the last event in a rapid sequence, following a pause of the configured delay. Throttling instead guarantees the function runs regardless of how many events fire in between — it doesn't wait for things to stop, it just rate-limits how often the handler executes during continuous activity. A search-as-you-type input is the classic debounce use case: you don't want to fire an API call on every keystroke, only once the user pauses typing, since intermediate partial queries are wasted work. A scroll or resize handler (e.g., updating a 'sticky header is visible' state, or lazy-loading images as you scroll) is a better fit for throttling, since you generally want periodic updatescontinuous scrolling, not just a single update after the user stops scrolling entirely — throttling every 100-200ms keeps the UI reasonably responsive to ongoing movement without running expensive work on every single scroll event (which can fire dozens of times per second).

questions.question: How would you use the React DevTools Profiler to find out which component is causing a performance problem, and what would you look for in the flame graph?
questions.answer: The Profiler tab (in the React DevTools browser extension) records a session while you interact with the app, then shows a 'flame graph' (or 'ranked' view) per committed render: each bar represents a component, its width roughly proportional to how long it took to render, and its color intensity indicating relative render duration compared to siblings. To diagnose a specific interaction, start recording, perform the slow interaction (e.g., typing in a field, opening a panel), stop recording, and step through each commit — look for components that re-rendered but shouldn't have (visible because they show up in a commit even though their visible output didn't change), components with unusually wide bars (expensive renders worth investigating or memoizing), and commits that include far more components than the interaction should have touched (a sign state was lifted too high, or a Context value is triggering broad re-renders). The Profiler can also show, for each rendered component, why it re-rendered (props changed, state changed, hooks changed, parent re-rendered) in recent React DevTools versions, which is usually the fastest path to the actual root cause rather than guessing.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS (styled-components/Emotion), and utility-first CSS (Tailwind) for styling a React app?
questions.answer: CSS Modules are plain CSS files with locally-scoped class names (compiled to unique hashes to avoid collisions), imported into components — you get real CSS (all selectors, media queries, pseudo-classes work exactly as in CSS) with zero runtime cost, predictable browser caching of the CSS file, and straightforward SSR, but dynamic/prop-driven styling requires manually toggling class names or falling back to inline styles. CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) lets you write styles as JS template literals or objects colocated with the component, making prop-driven dynamic styles very natural (`background: ${props => props.color}`) and enabling powerful theming — but classic 'runtime' CSS-in-JS injects `<style>` tags at render time, which has a real performance cost (extra work per render, larger JS bundle since styles ship as JS) and historically complicated SSR (needing to extract and inject critical CSS server-side, with extra setup). Utility-first CSS (Tailwind) applies small, single-purpose classes directly in markup, avoiding both the naming problem of hand-written CSS and CSS-in-JS's runtime cost (Tailwind is a build-time tool generating a static stylesheet) — the trade-off is verbose/cluttered JSX class strings and a learning curve for the utility vocabulary, though many teams find it speeds up iteration once adopted. Newer 'zero-runtime' CSS-in-JS tools (vanilla-extract, Linaria, Panda CSS) try to combine CSS-in-JS's developer ergonomics with build-time extraction to avoid the runtime cost, splitting the difference between the first two approaches.

questions.question: What issues can CSS-in-JS libraries cause for server-side rendering or runtime performance, and how do 'zero-runtime' CSS-in-JS approaches try to fix that?
questions.answer: Traditional ('runtime') CSS-in-JS libraries compute and inject styles while the app runs — during SSR this means the server has to render the component tree, collect every style rule that was generated along the way, and inject a `<style>` tag into the HTML response before sending it, which adds server-side work and setup complexity (each library has its own SSR extraction API to wire up correctly, and getting it wrong causes a flash of unstyled content or a hydration mismatch on styles). On the client, generating and injecting styles at render time (parsing template literals or style objects, computing class names, inserting/updating stylesheet rules) adds per-render overhead that a static CSS file simply doesn't have, and ships the styling logic itself as part of the JS bundle rather than a separately-cacheable CSS file. 'Zero-runtime' CSS-in-JS tools (vanilla-extract, Linaria, Compiled, Panda CSS) address this by moving style computation to build time: you still write styles colocated with components in a CSS-in-JS-like syntax, but a build-time compiler extracts them into real static `.css` files ahead of time, so there's no runtime style-injection cost and no special SSR extraction step needed — you get colocated, type-safe styling with plain CSS's performance and caching characteristics, at the cost of losing some fully-dynamic runtime capabilities that pure runtime libraries support (like styles computed from arbitrary runtime values that aren't known until render).

questions.question: How would you structure a large React codebase — by file type (components/, hooks/, utils/) or by feature/domain — and what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer: By file type (a global `components/`, `hooks/`, `utils/`, `pages/` at the top level) is simple and familiar for small apps, but as an app grows, related code for a single feature ends up scattered across many top-level folders — adding or understanding one feature requires jumping between distant directories, and it becomes hard to tell what's safe to delete or which components are actually feature-specific versus genuinely shared. By feature/domain (a `features/checkout/`, `features/dashboard/` structure, each containing its own components, hooks, API calls, and types) keeps everything related to one piece of functionality colocated, making it far easier to reason about, onboard onto, or even extract into a separate package/micro-frontend later; a small number of genuinely cross-cutting things (a design system, shared utilities/hooks used by many features) still live in a top-level `shared/` or `common/` folder. The trade-off is mostly upfront discipline: feature-based structure requires deciding, sometimes ambiguously, whether something belongs in a feature folder or in `shared/`, and can encourage some duplication if teams default to feature-local code rather than checking for existing shared utilities. For anything beyond a small app, feature/domain-based organization is now the more commonly recommended default, especially in teams working on the same codebase in parallel.

questions.question: What is micro-frontend architecture, and what problem is it trying to solve for large organizations with multiple teams shipping to the same site?
questions.answer: Micro-frontends extend the microservices idea to the frontend: instead of one large, monolithic frontend codebase owned by everyone, a site/app is decomposed into smaller, independently-built and independently-deployable pieces (sometimes owned by different teams, potentially even using different frameworks or versions of React), which are composed together at runtime or build time into one experience for the end user. The problem it addresses is organizational scale: a single large React app shared by many teams tends to accumulate a shared, coupled dependency graph, a single CI/deploy pipeline that becomes a bottleneck, and merge/coordination overhead when many teams touch the same codebase simultaneously — micro-frontends let each team ship on its own schedule, with its own tech choices, without blocking or being blocked by other teams' releases. Common implementation approaches include Webpack Module Federation (loading remote, independently-built bundles at runtime) and `single-spa` (a framework-agnostic orchestrator for mounting/unmounting independently-built apps into shared regions of a page). The trade-offs are real: potential duplication of shared dependencies (e.g., multiple React instances shipped unless carefully shared), more complex tooling/CI, harder-to-guarantee UI/UX consistency across teams, and genuinely added architectural complexity — most teams should only reach for this once organizational scale actually justifies it, not by default.

questions.question: You have a form component that re-renders on every keystroke and starts lagging on a large form — how would you diagnose and fix it?
questions.answer: First confirm the actual cost with the React DevTools Profiler: record while typing in the laggy field and check whether the re-render is scoped to just that field or whether the entire form (including many unrelated sibling fields) re-renders on every keystroke — the latter is the usual culprit and points to state being held too high (e.g., one big `useState` object for the whole form, where updating any field's value triggers a re-render of every field's rendering logic if they're not individually memoized). Fixes, roughly in order of effort: (1) if using a controlled-forms library, switch to (or configure) uncontrolled-by-default handling — React Hook Form's `register()` approach avoids most of this by design, since typing doesn't trigger React re-renders of sibling fields at all; (2) split monolithic form state into per-field local state (or field-scoped context) so only the field actually being typed in re-renders; (3) wrap expensive sibling components (a live preview panel, a complex validation-summary component) in `React.memo` so they don't re-render just because a keystroke changed unrelated state; (4) if per-keystroke validation is itself expensive (e.g., a complex schema check), debounce it so it doesn't run synchronously on every character.

questions.question: A component's useEffect is firing in an infinite loop — what are the most common causes, and how would you track down which dependency is the culprit?
questions.answer: The usual root cause: the effect updates some state that is itself (directly or via a derived value) in its own dependency array, so the update triggers a re-render, which re-runs the effect, which updates state again, forever. The most common concrete forms are: an object or array created fresh on every render being listed as a dependency (its reference is 'new' every time even if the contents are equivalent, so the effect sees it as 'changed' every render); a function prop that isn't memoized being called inside the effect and also listed as a dependency; or the effect calling a state setter unconditionally instead of only when the new value actually differs from the current one. To track down which dependency is responsible: temporarily log each dependency's value (and whether it's `Object.is`-equal to the previous render's value) right before the effect runs, or use a small custom hook like `useWhyDidYouUpdate`/the `why-did-you-render` library to print which prop/state changed between renders. Once identified, the fix is usually either wrapping the offending value in `useMemo`/`useCallback` so its reference is stable across renders when its contents haven't changed, or restructuring the effect so it doesn't need that value as a dependency at all (e.g., using the state updater's functional form instead of reading the current state value).

questions.question: Users report that a page briefly shows the wrong content before 'flashing' to the correct content after load — what's likely happening, and how would you fix it (hydration mismatch scenario)?
questions.answer: This is a classic symptom of a hydration mismatch: the server rendered one version of the HTML, but on the client, React's first render (before any effects have run) produces different output — the browser initially displays the server's HTML, then React hydrates and, on detecting the mismatch, replaces it with what the client actually computed, causing a visible flash. Common causes: reading `localStorage`, a cookie, or `window`-dependent values (like `window.innerWidth`) synchronously during render to decide what to show, when those values are only available client-side and differ from whatever the server assumed; date/time or locale formatting that differs between server and client environments; or conditionally rendering based on something like `typeof window !== 'undefined'` directly in the render body. The fix is to ensure the first client render matches the server output exactly, and defer any client-only logic to run after that first render — typically by initializing state with the server-safe default, then updating it inside a `useEffect` (which only runs client-side, after hydration) once the real client-only value is available, accepting that there will be one extra render pass after mount rather than a mismatched initial paint. For content that's genuinely meant to differ between server and client (like time-zone-adjusted timestamps), some teams intentionally suppress the specific mismatch warning on that element while still fixing everything else, though matching output is the more robust default.

questions.question: A list re-renders every item even though only one item's data changed — walk through how you'd figure out why memoization isn't working.
questions.answer: Start by confirming the symptom with the Profiler: record while triggering the single-item update and check whether every list-item component actually re-renders (not just the parent list container, which re-rendering is expected and fine). If every item component does re-render, the most likely cause is that the item components aren't wrapped in `React.memo` at all — a plain function component re-renders whenever its parent does, regardless of whether its own props changed, so if the list array itself is a new reference every render (e.g., `items.map(...)` producing a new array from a `.filter()`/`.sort()` computed inline in the parent's render body), the parent re-rendering cascades to every child by default. If the items are wrapped in `React.memo` but still all re-render, check what's being passed as props: an inline arrow function passed as an `onClick`/`onChange` prop to each item, or an inline object/array prop, creates a new reference on every parent render — `React.memo`'s shallow comparison sees this as 'changed' for every item, defeating the memoization. The fix is typically to memoize any callbacks passed to list items with `useCallback` (parameterized by item ID, or using event delegation so the same stable callback works for all items), memoize any object/array props with `useMemo`, and ensure the memoized item component itself correctly wraps with `React.memo`.

questions.question: How would you design a state management approach for a real-time collaborative feature (e.g., multiple users editing the same document)?
questions.answer: Model state as coming from two sources that need reconciling: local optimistic edits (what the current user just typed/changed, shown immediately for responsiveness) and remote updates streaming in from other users (typically via WebSockets or a similar real-time transport). A naive 'last write wins' approach where every keystroke is broadcast and blindly overwrites shared state causes edits to clobber each other when two users type concurrently; production collaborative editors instead use conflict-resolution algorithms — either Operational Transformation (OT, used by Google Docs) or, more commonly in newer implementations, CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, used by libraries like Yjs or Automerge) — which let concurrent edits from multiple clients merge deterministically without a central lock, and which integrate with React via a store/provider (e.g., Yjs's React bindings) that components subscribe to like any other state source. On the state-management side: keep the 'document' state in a store separate from ephemeral per-user UI state (cursor position, selection, presence indicators — often synced via a lighter-weight, more frequent channel than the actual document content), use `useSyncExternalStore` (React's hook designed exactly for subscribing to external, non-React-owned state sources) to bridge the CRDT/store's updates into React re-renders correctly, and design the network layer to reconnect and resync gracefully after a dropped connection rather than assuming the WebSocket is always connected.

questions.question: How would you approach building a design system / shared component library that multiple product teams consume, and what makes an API 'hard to misuse'?
questions.answer: Structurally, most design systems separate primitive/headless behavior (accessibility, keyboard handling, state logic — e.g., what Radix UI or React Aria provide) from visual styling (your org's specific look), so consuming teams get correct accessible behavior 'for free' while still being able to theme it to match brand guidelines; building both from scratch is a much larger undertaking than most product teams should take on themselves. A 'hard to misuse' API generally means: sensible, safe defaults so a component behaves reasonably with minimal props supplied; the compound-component pattern for complex components (Tabs, Menu, Accordion) so structure is explicit and composable rather than one component with dozens of boolean flags controlling every possible configuration; TypeScript types that make invalid prop combinations a compile error rather than a silent runtime bug (as discussed for mutually-exclusive props); and consistent naming/behavior conventions across the whole library so learning one component transfers to the next. Beyond the API itself, a design system needs real infrastructure to stay usable at scale: visual regression testing (Chromatic/Storybook) to catch unintended UI changes, a documented versioning/deprecation policy so consuming teams aren't broken by silent updates, and genuine ownership/governance so requests for new components or breaking changes go through a clear process rather than ad hoc forking.

questions.question: How would you decide, for a new project in 2026, between plain React + a router/query library versus a full framework like Next.js or Remix/React Router v7?
questions.answer: A framework (Next.js App Router, Remix/React Router v7 in framework mode, TanStack Start) buys you an opinionated, integrated setup for the things almost every real app needs eventually: file-based or config-based routing, data loading co-located with routes (loaders/actions), built-in support for Server Components/Server Actions where relevant, SSR/streaming, image and font optimization, and a production build pipeline tuned for these patterns — considerably less glue code and fewer decisions than assembling Vite + React Router + a data-fetching library + a manual SSR setup by hand. The trade-off is more 'magic'/convention to learn, tighter coupling to that framework's specific patterns and release cadence, and sometimes more constraint on deployment targets. Plain React (a Vite/CRA-successor SPA setup) with React Router and TanStack Query remains a reasonable choice when the app is genuinely client-only (an internal admin tool, a dashboard behind auth where SEO and first-paint don't matter, or an app embedded in another shell like an Electron app or browser extension), when the team wants maximal control over the build pipeline, or when the project is small enough that a framework's extra structure isn't earning its complexity yet. For anything public-facing where SEO, initial load performance, or server-rendered data fetching genuinely matter, a framework is generally the stronger default in the current React ecosystem, given how much of the React team's own guidance and new features (Server Components, Actions) assume a framework is present.

questions.question: What is React, and what problem does it solve compared to manipulating the DOM directly?
questions.answer: React is a declarative, component-based JavaScript library (created at Facebook/Meta) for building user interfaces. Before React, most UIs were built with imperative DOM manipulation — you had to manually track which DOM nodes existed and write code to update them step by step whenever data changed, which becomes error-prone and hard to reason about as an app grows. React instead lets you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and it works out how to update the real DOM efficiently (via a lightweight in-memory representation and a diffing/reconciliation process). This declarative model, combined with reusable components, one-way data flow, and hooks for stateful logic, makes UI code more predictable, testable, and easier to reason about, and it works across web (React DOM), mobile (React Native), and server rendering.

questions.question: What's the difference between a React element, a React node, and a component?
questions.answer: A React element is the plain, immutable JavaScript object produced by JSX or `React.createElement()` — it describes what should be rendered (a type, props, and children) but is not the actual DOM. A component is a function (or, historically, a class) that accepts props and returns elements/nodes; it's the reusable definition, not a rendered instance. A React node is the broader umbrella term for anything React can actually render: an element, a string, a number, an array of nodes, a fragment, a portal, or the booleans `null`/`undefined`/`true`/`false` (which render as nothing). In short: components are factories, elements are the objects they produce, and nodes are the full set of renderable values, including elements.

questions.question: What's the difference between props and state?
questions.answer: Props are data passed into a component from its parent — they're read-only from the receiving component's perspective, and the component re-renders when the parent passes new props. State is data a component owns internally and can update itself, typically via `useState`/`useReducer`; changing state triggers that component (and its subtree) to re-render. Together they implement React's one-way data flow: state lives at whichever component is the lowest common ancestor that needs it, gets passed down as props to children, and any changes flow back up via callback props the parent supplied. A common mistake is trying to derive state from props with `useState` and an effect — usually it's simpler and more correct to just compute the derived value during render.

questions.question: Why does React recommend against mutating state directly, and what actually breaks if you do?
questions.answer: Several core React mechanisms rely on reference (not deep) equality to detect change. `useState`/`useReducer` bail out of a re-render if the new state is `Object.is`-equal to the old one; `React.memo`, and dependency arrays in `useMemo`/`useCallback`/`useEffect`, compare previous vs. next values by reference. If you mutate an object or array in place and pass the same reference back to a setter, React may not detect that anything changed, so the UI silently fails to update, or updates inconsistently since some parts of the tree still hold the old (now-mutated) object. Mutation also breaks time-travel debugging in React DevTools and can cause subtle bugs under concurrent rendering, where React may keep multiple versions of state around. The fix is to always produce a new object/array (spread syntax, `map`/`filter`/`toSorted`, or a helper library like Immer) and pass that to the state setter.

questions.question: What's the purpose of the key prop when rendering lists, and why shouldn't you default to the array index?
questions.answer: `key` tells React how to match a rendered child to a specific piece of data across re-renders, so it can reuse (rather than destroy and recreate) the right component instance, preserve its internal state, and correctly reorder DOM nodes. Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not globally. Using the array index as the key works fine for static lists that never reorder, insert, or remove items, but breaks down otherwise: because the key represents a position rather than an identity, if you insert an item at the top or remove one from the middle, React ends up reusing the wrong component instance for the wrong data — this manifests as stale local state, wrong input values, or lost focus attached to the wrong row. The fix is to use a stable, unique field from the data itself (like a database ID).

questions.question: What's the difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled input, and when would you choose each?
questions.answer: A controlled input has its value driven entirely by React state: you pass `value`/`checked` and update it via `onChange`, so React state is the single source of truth and you can validate, transform, or conditionally render based on every keystroke. An uncontrolled input lets the DOM keep its own value; you read it via a `ref` (typically on submit) and can set an initial value with `defaultValue`/`defaultChecked`. Controlled inputs are the default choice when you need live validation, conditionally-derived UI, or to keep multiple fields in sync. Uncontrolled inputs are simpler for write-once/submit-only forms and are required for `<input type="file">`, which the browser always manages itself. React 19 also added first-class form primitives (the `action` prop on `<form>`, `useFormStatus`, `useActionState`) that can reduce the need for per-field controlled state in many form-handling scenarios.
